title: Data
text:
The dataset captures hazardous cargo (HNS — Hazardous and Noxious Substances) handled at Turkish ports during 2022. It was published by the Directorate General for Maritime Affairs (T.C. Ulaştırma ve Altyapı Bakanlığı – Denizcilik Genel Müdürlüğü) and shared with us in the form of a pivot-table workbook prepared by the directorate’s intern team.
Each leaf record describes a single cargo movement at the resolution of:

the regional port authority (e.g., Aliağa Bölge Liman Başkanlığı),
the facility that handled the cargo (e.g., Egegaz Aliağa LNG Terminal),
the receiver / final consignee company,
the cargo amount in metric tons.



We chose it for three reasons:

It’s real, operational, and Turkish. No simulated toy data — the patterns we surface are about the actual industrial geography of Türkiye’s coastlines.
It supports policy questions. The Maritime Affairs office has flagged firms handling more than 20,000 tons of hazardous cargo as candidates for upcoming tax/regulatory measures. The dataset lets us put numbers on that conversation.
It’s multi-dimensional. Company × facility × port authority gives us room for descriptive, geographic, and threshold-based analyses without leaving a single source.

title: Data
text:
Source

Directorate General for Maritime Affairs. 2022 Hazardous Cargo Handling Records. Internal compilation, accessed via project supervisor.

The original Excel workbook is bundled with this site as data/HNS_2022.xlsx, alongside the cleaned versions described below.

title: Data
text:
Preparation pipeline
The raw workbook is a pivot-table export with three nested categorical levels (port authority → facility → company) and built-in subtotal rows (“Toplam …”). To analyse it we need a flat, tidy table.
The full preprocessing script lives at R/prepare_data.R. In short, it:

Reads the workbook with readxl::read_excel() and assigns clean column names: port_authority, facility, company, cargo_mt.
Drops every subtotal row (Toplam …) at all three hierarchy levels.
Drops rows where the company or tonnage is missing.
Renames the (boş) placeholder facility (used at Güllük) to Unspecified facility.
Builds a company_clean field — uppercased, ASCII-folded, punctuation-stripped — for grouping near-duplicate company names.
Extracts a port_authority_short field by stripping the boilerplate “Bölge Liman Başkanlığı” suffix.
Joins a province + ISO-2 code lookup so we can map each port authority onto a Turkish province for the choropleth.

Re-run the script any time the source workbook changes:
source("R/prepare_data.R")
It writes:

data/HNS_2022_clean.RData — the canonical R object.
data/HNS_2022_clean.csv — the same table in CSV (UTF-8) for inspection / sharing.

overview



  





215 Records


17 Port authorities


69 Facilities


180 Companies (cleaned)

The dataset is a long table where each row pairs a receiver company with the facility that handled their cargo and the regional port authority that oversees that facility. The numeric column cargo_mt is what we’ll be slicing in every direction below.

title: Analysis
section: 2. Where is hazardous cargo concentrated? — Türkiye choropleth
text:
2. Where is hazardous cargo concentrated? — Türkiye choropleth
We map each regional port authority onto its host province and sum 2022 tonnage by province. Darker = more cargo.


Show code
prov_totals <- hns2022 |>
  group_by(iso2, province) |>
  summarise(total_mt = sum(cargo_mt), .groups = "drop")

tr_states <- ne_states(country = "Turkey", returnclass = "sf")

if ("iso_3166_2" %in% names(tr_states)) {
  tr_map <- tr_states |>
    left_join(prov_totals, by = c("iso_3166_2" = "iso2"))
} else {
  norm <- function(x) tolower(stringi::stri_trans_general(x, "Any-Latin; Latin-ASCII"))
  tr_map <- tr_states |>
    mutate(name_n = norm(name)) |>
    left_join(prov_totals |> mutate(name_n = norm(province)), by = "name_n")
}

ggplot(tr_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = total_mt), color = "white", linewidth = 0.35) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours  = c("#F06292", "#EC407A", "#E91E63", "#C2185B", "#880E4F", "#3D0823"),
    na.value = "#9C8D88",
    labels   = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale()),
    name     = "Cargo (m. ton)"
  ) +
  coord_sf(crs = 4326) +
  labs(
    title    = "Türkiye's hazardous cargo, 2022",
    subtitle = "Provinces are filled by the total tonnage handled at port authorities they host. Grey = no port authority in that province.",
    caption  = "Source: Directorate General for Maritime Affairs, 2022. Author calculations."
  ) +
  theme_void(base_family = "Inter") +
  theme(
    plot.title       = element_text(family = "Playfair Display", face = "italic", size = 22,
                                    color = "#3D0823", margin = margin(b = 6)),
    plot.subtitle    = element_text(color = "#3D0823", size = 12, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.caption     = element_text(color = "#3D0823", size = 10, hjust = 0,
                                    margin = margin(t = 8)),
    legend.title     = element_text(color = "#3D0823", face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.text      = element_text(color = "#3D0823", size = 10),
    legend.position  = "right",
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#FFFAF7", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFAF7", color = NA)
  )





Total hazardous cargo handled in 2022, by host province of the port authority. Darker = more cargo.




The Aegean coast (especially İzmir, which hosts both Aliağa and the İzmir port authority) and the Eastern Mediterranean (Adana’s Ceyhan terminals and Hatay’s İskenderun) carry most of the load. The Black Sea, Marmara, and Antalya regions show meaningful but smaller volumes.

title: Analysis
section: 3. How is cargo distributed across companies? — density plot
text:
3. How is cargo distributed across companies? — density plot
Aggregating to company-level totals and plotting the density on a log axis:


Show code
company_totals <- hns2022 |>
  group_by(company_clean) |>
  summarise(total_mt = sum(cargo_mt), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(total_mt > 0)

ggplot(company_totals, aes(x = total_mt)) +
  geom_density(fill = "#FF80B0", alpha = 0.55, color = "#C2185B", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 20000, linetype = "dashed", color = "#00C9D8", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = 20000, y = Inf,
    label = "20,000-ton threshold",
    vjust = 1.5, hjust = -0.05,
    color = "#00838F", fill = "#FFFAF7",
    label.size = 0,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(
    title    = "Most companies are small. A handful are enormous.",
    subtitle = "Density of company-level total tonnage in 2022 (log-10 axis).",
    x = "Total cargo per company (metric tons, log scale)",
    y = "Density",
    caption = "Each company aggregated by its cleaned, deduplicated name."
  ) +
  theme_riyo()


Warning in annotate("label", x = 20000, y = Inf, label = "20,000-ton
threshold", : Ignoring unknown parameters: `label.size`





Density of total 2022 hazardous-cargo tonnage per company (log scale). The cyan dashed line is the 20,000-ton policy threshold.




The shape is unmistakable: a long left tail of small handlers, a clear hump in the 10³–10⁴ ton range, then a thin upper tail extending well past 10⁷ tons. Viewed on a linear axis the small companies would be invisible — they’re outnumbered by but dwarfed in volume by a few giants.

title: Analysis
section: 4. The 20,000-ton question — a hypothetical tax simulation
text:
4. The 20,000-ton question — a hypothetical tax simulation
The Directorate is considering tax/regulatory measures targeting companies that exceed 20,000 tons of hazardous cargo per year. To put a number on what that would mean, we apply a hypothetical ₺50 per ton levy on the full tonnage of any company that crosses the threshold.

Disclaimer. ₺50/ton is illustrative — chosen for arithmetic clarity, not based on any draft policy. Treat absolute figures as proportions, not forecasts.



Show code
TAX_RATE_TL_PER_TON <- 50

co_tax <- company_totals |>
  mutate(
    above_threshold = total_mt > 20000,
    tax_TL = if_else(above_threshold, total_mt * TAX_RATE_TL_PER_TON, 0)
  )

threshold_summary <- co_tax |>
  summarise(
    n_total          = n(),
    n_taxed          = sum(above_threshold),
    pct_companies    = mean(above_threshold) * 100,
    total_mt         = sum(total_mt),
    taxed_mt         = sum(total_mt[above_threshold]),
    pct_taxed_mt     = sum(total_mt[above_threshold]) / sum(total_mt) * 100,
    total_tax_TL     = sum(tax_TL),
    total_tax_billion= sum(tax_TL) / 1e9
  )

threshold_summary



  





Show code
share_df <- tibble(
  metric = factor(
    c("Companies", "Tonnage moved"),
    levels = c("Companies", "Tonnage moved")
  ),
  above  = c(threshold_summary$pct_companies,           threshold_summary$pct_taxed_mt),
  below  = c(100 - threshold_summary$pct_companies, 100 - threshold_summary$pct_taxed_mt)
) |>
  pivot_longer(c(above, below), names_to = "side", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(side = factor(side, levels = c("below", "above"),
                       labels = c("Below 20k tons", "Above 20k tons")))

ggplot(share_df, aes(x = metric, y = pct, fill = side)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", pct)),
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
    color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 5,
    family = "Inter"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Below 20k tons" = "#FFC1D8", "Above 20k tons" = "#C2185B")) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title    = "Wide net, top-heavy bill.",
    subtitle = sprintf(
      "%.0f%% of companies cross the 20,000-ton threshold — and together they account for ~%.1f%% of all hazardous tonnage.",
      threshold_summary$pct_companies, threshold_summary$pct_taxed_mt
    ),
    x = NULL, y = "Share (%)", fill = NULL,
    caption = "₺50/ton hypothetical levy applied to crossing companies only."
  ) +
  theme_riyo() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

How many companies exceed the threshold — and what share of total tonnage they account for.






Show code
top10_tax <- co_tax |>
  filter(above_threshold) |>
  slice_max(tax_TL, n = 10) |>
  mutate(
    label_short = str_trunc(company_clean, 38),
    label_short = fct_reorder(label_short, tax_TL)
  )

ggplot(top10_tax, aes(x = label_short, y = tax_TL / 1e6)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#C2185B", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = scales::label_number(accuracy = 1, big.mark = ",")(tax_TL / 1e6)),
    hjust = -0.15, color = "#2A0E33", family = "Inter", fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(suffix = "M ₺"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Where the bill would land — top 10 hypothetical taxpayers",
    subtitle = sprintf(
      "Total industry liability ≈ ₺%.1f billion · top 10 share ≈ %.0f%%",
      threshold_summary$total_tax_billion,
      sum(top10_tax$tax_TL) / threshold_summary$total_tax_TL * 100
    ),
    x = NULL, y = "Hypothetical tax (million ₺)",
    caption = "Hypothetical levy: ₺50 per ton on companies above 20,000 tons of 2022 hazardous cargo."
  ) +
  theme_riyo()





Ten largest hypothetical taxpayers under a ₺50/ton levy on companies above 20,000 tons.




The top ten alone shoulder the majority of the bill. The next several dozen companies above the threshold pay meaningful but much smaller amounts; everyone else pays nothing under this design.

Sensitivity to the threshold
What if the threshold weren’t 20,000 tons? The plot below traces how the number of taxpayers and the share of tonnage taxed move as we slide it.


Show code
thresholds <- c(5e3, 1e4, 2e4, 5e4, 1e5, 2.5e5, 5e5, 1e6)

sens <- tibble(threshold = thresholds) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    n_taxed     = sum(company_totals$total_mt > threshold),
    share_mt    = sum(company_totals$total_mt[company_totals$total_mt > threshold]) /
                  sum(company_totals$total_mt) * 100
  ) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(sens, aes(x = threshold)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = share_mt), color = "#C2185B", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = share_mt), color = "#C2185B", size = 3) +
  geom_text(
    aes(y = share_mt, label = sprintf("n=%d", n_taxed)),
    vjust = -1, color = "#00838F", fontface = "bold", size = 3.4, family = "Inter"
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",", scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 105), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(
    title    = "How sharp is the cliff at 20,000 tons?",
    subtitle = "Even a 5x or 10x stricter threshold barely loses tonnage coverage — the giants dominate.",
    x = "Threshold (metric tons, log scale)",
    y = "Share of total tonnage above threshold",
    caption = "Annotations show the number of companies caught at each threshold."
  ) +
  theme_riyo()





Sensitivity of the policy to the threshold value.




The take-away: because the upper tail is so heavy, moving the threshold up by an order of magnitude barely reduces tonnage coverage — but it sharply reduces the number of companies subject to the policy. That’s a useful lever for designers who want a high-impact, low-friction policy.

title: Analysis
text:
6. Conclusions

Geography: Türkiye’s hazardous cargo handling is not evenly distributed. A small set of provinces — driven by refining and large export terminals — dominates national volume.
Industry structure: The market is a classic heavy-tailed distribution. Many small handlers, a few giants moving most of the tonnage.
Policy implication: Because volume is so concentrated, a tonnage-based levy is administratively narrow — it would touch a minority of companies but capture most of the activity. That makes it both easy to enforce and politically charged.
Sensitivity: Moving the threshold from 20,000 to 100,000 or 200,000 tons would not meaningfully reduce coverage of total tonnage but would significantly reduce the number of regulated firms — a real lever for policy designers.

Visit our Data page for documentation and the cleaned dataset, and the Team page to meet the people behind it.
Code

The project
Turkish ports moved tens of millions of tons of hazardous cargo in 2022 — fertilizers, fuels, chemicals, LPG, crude oil. We took the Directorate General for Maritime Affairs operational dataset for that year and asked three questions:

Where is hazardous cargo concentrated geographically?
Who are the dominant handlers — and how skewed is the distribution?
What would happen if Türkiye taxed companies that exceeded a 20,000-ton threshold?

Our group name R’ıyo is a nod to Manifest’s “Arıyo” — in Turkish the letter R reads “ar”, so R’ıyo = Arıyo. Six members, six energies, one dataset.

Key takeaways

Hazardous cargo handling in 2022 totaled ~109 million metric tons across 17 port authorities, 69 facilities and 180 receiver companies — a small slice of firms handles a wildly disproportionate share.
The Aliağa–İzmir corridor and Ceyhan lead by a wide margin, driven by refining and crude-oil terminals; the Eastern Mediterranean and South Marmara coasts form a clear secondary band.
The distribution of company-level tonnage is strongly right-skewed even on a log axis — a handful of giants extend far past 10⁷ tons while most receivers cluster in the 10³–10⁴ range.
Six in ten companies (107 of 180) cross the 20,000-ton policy threshold — and together they carry ~99.5% of all hazardous tonnage. The policy net is wide by headcount but extremely top-heavy in actual liability.
A simple hypothetical levy of ₺50 per ton on threshold-exceeding companies would raise about ₺5.4 billion in annual revenue — with the top ten handlers alone contributing the majority of that bill.

What’s next

The Data page documents the dataset, source, preprocessing, and link to the cleaned .RData.
The Analysis page is the main read — Türkiye choropleth, company distribution, and the 20,000-ton tax simulation.
